items.title: Nancy Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995
items.q: I do believe that was with Rusty Bryant’s band... I didn’t join that band until after high school... Rusty Bryant and our band started that whole midwest influx

ctx.x: He, there’s been a few people in your career that in the beginning were instrumental I think, and he was one and John Levy.
But before John Levy, and before Cannonball, there was a band called The Rusty Bryant band who recorded for Dot. And I understand there is a copy of a bootleg, because I © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

never signed with Dot. There is supposed to be a record out of me, somewhere, on Dot. And I do believe that was with Rusty Bryant’s band. And before Rusty Bryant, because I didn’t join that band until after high school, there was a band called Sir Raleigh Randolph and his Sultans of Swing. I was fifteen, and the band’s singer. And I played all the cabarets with — in the midwest and in Ohio. I felt really blessed to do that. It was unbelievable to be able to sing all those wonderful songs at a young, very young…

items.title: Nancy Wilson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I was working with Rusty Bryant... I played the Club Regal with Rusty a lot... Rusty Bryant and Nancy Wilson kind of established [the 502]

ctx.x: Was there much experience in your childhood or at school of segregation or issues of . . . ?

No, none. I didn’t go through that at all. I talked to some people that I went to school with since then. They seemed to think that there was segregation. They couldn’t be this and they couldn’t – but I don’t understand that, because I was – I had a French – I was vice president of the French club. I was the only black in drama. See, so I don’t know that it was anything that was there, because I did anything – everything that I wanted to do and did not get a sense of that. The first club I went to that I found…
Any family activities, fond memories of? What did you do in the summertime?
